meta.title: Four-day weeks and the division of unpaid labour in dual-earner households

primary.text: To what extent does a four-day working week change the division of unpaid labour between partners in dual-earner households in Belgium?
primary.tertium_comparationis: the share of unpaid household and care hours performed by each partner, before and after the transition
primary.scope: Dual-earner households in Belgium with at least one child under 12, in organisations that adopt a four-day week between 2027 and 2031.
primary.completion_criterion: The question is answered when the change in each partner's share of unpaid hours is estimated with a difference-in-differences design and the estimate is distinguishable from zero at conventional confidence.

method.approach: Quasi-experimental: difference-in-differences on household time-use diaries, with matched comparison households that stay on five days.

sources.description: Belgian time-use survey, 2022 wave, national statistical office release
Household diaries collected in adopting organisations, 2028 and 2030
Administrative payroll records, 2026-2031, for working-time verification

method.procedure: Recruit 40 adopting and 40 matched non-adopting households; collect seven-day diaries from both partners in each wave; code hours into paid work, housework, care and leisure; estimate partner shares with household fixed effects; test for anticipation one quarter before adoption.
validity_conditions: Households are observed before and after the transition with the same diary instrument
Comparison households are matched on sector, household composition and earnings
Attrition stays below 15 per cent per wave
limits: Findings describe dual-earner households with young children, not single-parent or childless households
The design cannot separate the four-day week from concurrent changes in organisational workload
Diary self-reports undercount short care episodes

warrant.gap_statement: Belgian time-use evidence stops at 2022 and predates the current wave of four-day-week pilots, so no study estimates the reallocation of unpaid hours within households after adoption.
evidence: Belgian time-use survey, 2022 wave, national statistical office release
OECD, Working time and the four-day week: evidence from pilots, 2023
FWO application form for a PhD fellowship, 2026
